notes.meaning: Hiram, the king of Tyre, sent messengers to congratulate Solomon on becoming king and to express sympathy after David's death. Hiram had been a loyal friend and admirer of King David for many years. This existing friendship paved the way for the two leaders to work together in peace.
Solomon sent a message back to Hiram to begin official discussions about temple building supplies. He wasted no time in putting their friendly alliance to work for God's honor.

Solomon explained why his father David had never built the temple. David spent his reign fighting wars against enemies on every side until God granted total victory. Because of all the bloodshed and conflict, God had reserved this holy building project for a time of peace.

Solomon celebrated the complete peace that God had granted him throughout the kingdom. There were no foreign attackers and no rebellions inside the country to distract him. He recognized that quiet, peaceful times are a gift from God to be used for His service.

Solomon announced his plan to build the temple in direct obedience to God's promise to David. God had told David that his son would sit on the throne and build a house for His Name. Building for God's "Name" meant creating a place where God's holy presence and character would be revealed and worshiped.

Solomon asked Hiram to cut cedar trees from the famous forests of Lebanon. With real humility, Solomon admitted that his own people were farmers and lacked the timber skills of the Sidonians. He promised to send Israelite helpers and to pay full wages for the work.

Hiram was overjoyed by Solomon's letter and praised the Lord for giving David such a wise son to rule Israel. Even if Hiram still held to pagan customs, David's godly life had given him deep respect for the true God. It brings great joy when wise leaders follow in the footsteps of faithful parents.

Hiram agreed to supply all the cedar and cypress wood Solomon wanted and proposed an efficient delivery plan. His workers would bind the logs into large sea rafts and float them down the Mediterranean coast to a port where Solomon could pick them up. In return, Hiram asked for grain and provisions to feed his royal court, since his coastal cities could not grow enough food.

Both kings honored their agreement faithfully year after year. Hiram provided all the timber Solomon requested, while Solomon shipped vast amounts of fine wheat and pure, crushed olive oil to feed Hiram's royal house. God used the different resources of each nation to meet the needs of both.

God gave Solomon great wisdom, exactly as He had promised, and it showed in his wise diplomacy and fair agreements. The two kings established a formal peace treaty and worked together in mutual trust. Godly wisdom brings people together in peace.

Solomon drafted a workforce of 30,000 men from among the Israelites to help secure the timber. This massive effort was only possible because Israel was at peace and had the energy to spare. The whole nation shared in the work of honoring God.

Solomon used a fair rotation system, sending 10,000 men to Lebanon for one month at a time, followed by two months at home. This allowed the men to care for their own farms and families rather than wearing them out with nonstop labor. An officer named Adoniram was placed in charge to keep the work organized and humane.

In addition to the Israelites, Solomon put 70,000 men to work carrying heavy loads and 80,000 to work cutting stone in the hill country. These laborers were mostly foreigners and descendants of the ancient peoples living in the land. Many commentators saw this foreign labor as a picture of Gentiles—people outside Israel—one day helping build God's spiritual church.

Solomon appointed 3,300 supervisors to manage the workers and keep the massive project running smoothly. Good management and oversight were necessary to guide such a huge workforce. God cares about order and good organization in His work.

The king ordered massive, costly stones to be cut and smoothed for the temple foundation. Even though these foundation stones would be buried underground and hidden from view, Solomon insisted on the best materials and finest craftsmanship. We should give God our best effort even in the parts of our service that no one else sees.

Masons from Israel worked alongside Hiram's builders and skilled craftsmen from the city of Gebal to shape the stones and prepare the beams. Together, they made every material ready for the construction of the Lord's house. This international effort showed that people from different nations could unite in service to the Lord.
